## Terms, partial sums and series {#ss2-terms-totals .terms-totals}

::: {.series-representation}
<div class="series-label">Sequence</div>

$$1,3,5,7,\ldots \qquad a_4=7$$

An ordered list. $a_n$ is **one term**.
:::

::: {.series-representation .fragment data-fragment-index="0"}
<div class="series-label">Partial sum</div>

$$S_n=a_1+a_2+\cdots+a_n \qquad S_4=1+3+5+7=16$$

$S_n$ is the sum of the **first $n$ terms**, for $n\ge1$.
:::

::: {.series-representation .fragment data-fragment-index="1"}
<div class="series-label">Infinite series</div>

$$1+3+5+7+\cdots$$

The sum of the terms of an infinite sequence.
:::

<p class="booklet-cue">Booklet pp. 5–6 · Partial sums and series</p>

::: notes
Next reveals the partial sum, then the infinite series. Distinguish commas from plus signs and a_n from S_n. A partial sum has finitely many terms; the corresponding infinite series continues indefinitely. A finite partial sum does not imply a finite limiting sum. This odd-number series has no finite limiting sum, but convergence belongs to a later lesson.
:::
